title: Chapter 26 — Some Considerations On War In Democratic Communities
paragraphs: When the principle of equality is growing not only within a single nation but across several neighboring nations at the same time, as is now the case in Europe, the inhabitants of these countries come to resemble one another in their shared dread of war and their common love of peace, however different their languages, customs and laws. *a Ambition or anger may put weapons in the hands of princes, but to no purpose: a general apathy and goodwill calms them in spite of themselves, the sword drops from their grasp, and wars become rarer. The spread of equality in several countries at once also impels their various inhabitants alike toward manufacturing and commerce. Their tastes then grow alike, and their interests become so mixed and entangled that no nation can do harm to others without the harm coming back on itself. In the end all nations see war as a calamity, almost as severe for the conqueror as for the conquered. So in democratic ages it is extremely difficult, on the one hand, to draw nations into hostilities; on the other hand, it is almost impossible for any two of them to go to war without involving the rest. The interests of all are so interlaced, and their opinions and needs so much alike, that none can stay quiet when the others are stirring. Wars therefore become rarer, but when they do break out they spread over a wider field. Neighboring democratic nations not only become alike in some respects; they end up resembling each other in almost all. *b This likeness between nations has very important consequences for war.

[Footnote a: I hardly need point out that the dread of war shown by the nations of Europe cannot be put down solely to the progress of the principle of equality among them. Besides this permanent cause, several accidental causes of great weight could be named, and above all of them I would place the extreme exhaustion left behind by the wars of the Revolution and the Empire.]

[Footnote b: This is not only because these nations share the same social condition; it comes from the very nature of that social condition, which leads men to imitate one another and identify with one another. When the members of a community are divided into castes and classes, they not only differ from one another but have no taste or desire to be alike. On the contrary, each person tries harder and harder to keep his own opinions undisturbed, to hold on to his own distinctive habits, and to remain himself. The characteristics of individuals are very strongly marked. When the state of society among a people is democratic — that is, when there are no longer any castes or classes in the community and all its members are nearly equal in education and in property — the human mind moves in the opposite direction. Men are much alike, and any departure from that likeness annoys them, as it were. Far from trying to preserve what is singular in themselves, they try to shake it off, so as to merge with the general mass of the people, which in their eyes is the sole representative of right and of might. The characteristics of individuals are nearly obliterated. In the ages of aristocracy, even people who are naturally alike strive to invent imaginary differences between themselves. In the ages of democracy, even people who are not alike seek only to become so and to copy each other, so strongly is every man’s mind swept along by the general impulse of mankind. Something of the same kind can be observed between nations. Two nations with the same aristocratic social condition might remain thoroughly distinct and very different, because the spirit of aristocracy is to keep strong individual characteristics. But if two neighboring nations have the same democratic social condition, they cannot fail to adopt similar opinions and customs, because the spirit of democracy tends to make men alike.]

Suppose I ask why the Helvetic Confederacy made the greatest and most powerful nations of Europe tremble in the fifteenth century, while today that country’s power is exactly proportioned to its population. I see that the Swiss have become like all the surrounding communities, and those surrounding communities like the Swiss. Since numerical strength is now the only difference between them, victory necessarily goes to the largest army. One consequence of the democratic revolution going on in Europe, then, is to make numerical strength prevail on every battlefield and to force all small nations either to merge with large States or at least to adopt their policy. Because numbers decide victory, every people ought of course to strive by every means in its power to put the greatest possible number of men in the field. When it was possible to recruit a kind of troops superior to all others, such as the Swiss infantry or the French cavalry of the sixteenth century, it was not thought necessary to raise very large armies. But matters change when one soldier is as good as another.

The same cause that creates this new need also supplies the means of meeting it. As I have already observed, when men are all alike they are all weak, and the supreme power of the state is naturally much stronger among democratic nations than elsewhere. So while these nations want to enroll the whole male population in the ranks of the army, they also have the power to do it. The result is that in democratic ages armies seem to grow larger as the love of war declines. In the same ages, the same causes also change the way war is waged. Machiavelli observes in “The Prince” “that it is much more difficult to subdue a people which has a prince and his barons for its leaders, than a nation which is commanded by a prince and his slaves.” To avoid giving offense, let us read “public officials” for “slaves,” and this important truth applies strictly to our own time.

A great aristocratic people can neither conquer its neighbors nor be conquered by them without great difficulty. It cannot conquer them, because it can never gather all its forces and hold them together for any considerable time. It cannot be conquered, because an enemy meets small centers of resistance at every step, and these stop the invasion. War against an aristocracy is like war in a mountainous country: the defeated side keeps finding chances to rally its forces and make a stand in a new position. Among democratic nations exactly the opposite occurs. They easily bring their whole available force into the field, and when the nation is wealthy and populous it soon wins. But if it is ever conquered and its territory invaded, it has few resources left to call on, and if the enemy takes the capital, the nation is lost. The reason is easy to see. Each member of the community is isolated and extremely powerless, so no one in the whole body can either defend himself or give others a point to rally around. Nothing in a democratic country is strong except the state. Once the destruction of the army has broken the state’s military strength and the capture of the chief city has paralyzed its civil power, all that remains is a multitude without strength or government, unable to resist the organized power attacking it. I am aware that the creation of provincial liberties, and with them provincial powers, can lessen this danger, but that remedy will always be insufficient. After such a catastrophe, not only is the population unable to continue the fighting, but one may fear that it will not even be inclined to try. Under the law of nations accepted in civilized countries, the object of wars is not to seize the property of private individuals but simply to take possession of political power. The destruction of private property is resorted to only occasionally, as a means to that end. When an aristocratic country is invaded after its army has been defeated, the nobles will go on defending themselves individually rather than submit, even though they are also the wealthiest members of the community. For if the conqueror remained master of the country, he would strip them of their political power, to which they cling even more closely than to their property. They therefore prefer fighting to subjection, which to them is the greatest of all misfortunes, and they readily carry the people along with them, because the people have long been used to following and obeying them and, besides, have little to risk in the war. Among a nation where equality of conditions prevails, by contrast, each citizen has only a slender share of political power, and often none at all. On the other hand, all are independent and all have something to lose. They are therefore much less afraid of being conquered, and much more afraid of war, than an aristocratic people. It will always be extremely difficult to persuade a democratic population to take up arms once hostilities have reached its own territory. Hence the necessity of giving such a people the rights and the political character that can give every citizen some of those interests which make the nobles act for the public welfare in aristocratic countries.

The princes and other leaders of democratic nations should never forget that only the passion and the habit of freedom can hold up successfully against the passion and the habit of physical well-being. I can imagine nothing better prepared for subjection, in the event of defeat, than a democratic people without free institutions.

In the past it was usual to take the field with a small body of troops, fight small engagements, and carry out long, regular sieges. Modern tactics consist in fighting decisive battles and, as soon as a line of march opens before the army, rushing on the capital city to end the war with a single blow. Napoleon, it is said, invented this new system. But its invention did not depend on any one man, whoever he might be. The state of society in his time suggested to Napoleon his way of making war. That way succeeded because it was admirably suited to that state of society, and because he was the first to use it. Napoleon was the first commander to march at the head of an army from capital to capital, but the ruin of feudal society had opened the road for him. It is fair to believe that if that extraordinary man had been born three hundred years ago, he would not have got the same results from his method of warfare — or rather, that he would have had a different method.

I will add only a few words on civil wars, for fear of exhausting the reader’s patience. Most of what I have said about foreign wars applies a fortiori to civil wars. Men who live in democracies are not naturally inclined to the military character. They sometimes take it on when they have been dragged into the field by compulsion. But rising in a body and voluntarily exposing themselves to the horrors of war, and especially civil war, is a course that the men of democracies are not apt to take. Only the most adventurous members of the community agree to run such risks; the bulk of the population stays motionless. Even if the population were inclined to act, considerable obstacles would stand in its way. It has no old, well-established influence that it is willing to obey, no well-known leaders to rally the discontented as well as to discipline and lead them, and no political powers subordinate to the supreme power of the nation that could give effective support to resistance directed against the government. In democratic countries the moral power of the majority is immense, and the physical resources at its command are out of all proportion to those that could be combined against it. Therefore the party that occupies the seat of the majority, speaks in its name and wields its power, triumphs instantly and irresistibly over all private resistance. It does not even give such opposition time to exist but nips it in the bud. Those who seek to bring about a revolution by force of arms in such nations have no other resource than suddenly to seize the whole machinery of government as it stands, and a single blow can do that better than a war. For as soon as a regular war begins, the party that represents the state is always certain to win. The only case in which a civil war could arise is if the army split into two factions, one raising the standard of rebellion and the other remaining loyal. An army is a small community, very closely united, endowed with great vitality, and able to supply its own needs for some time. Such a war might be bloody, but it could not be long. Either the rebellious army would win over the government by the mere display of its resources, or by its first victory, and then the war would be over; or the struggle would take place, and then the part of the army not supported by the organized powers of the state would quickly either disband or be destroyed. It may therefore be accepted as a general truth that in ages of equality civil wars will become much less frequent and shorter. *c

[Footnote c: Remember that I am speaking here of sovereign and independent democratic nations, not of confederate democracies. In confederacies the preponderant power always resides, in spite of all political fictions, in the state governments and not in the federal government, so civil wars are in fact nothing but foreign wars in disguise.]
